title: Higher-Order Functions
summary: Functions that take or return functions: composition, wrappers and callbacks.

steps.title: Functions in, functions out
body: A **higher-order function** takes a function, returns one, or both. You already used them: `map`, `filter` and `makeCounter`.
Typing them in TypeScript reads like the signature itself:
The `<T>` is a **generic**, just as in C#. Module 5 covers generics in depth.

code: const twice = (f: (n: number) => number) => (n: number) => f(f(n));

steps.title: Composition and pipelines
body: Composing small functions is a core JavaScript style:
const pipe = <T>(...fns: ((x: T) => T)[]) => (x: T) => fns.reduce((acc, f) => f(acc), x);
Wrappers that add behaviour around a function (logging, retry, caching) are just higher-order functions too. Next.js middleware and React hooks lean on exactly this idea.

steps.prompt: Complete `pipe` so functions run left to right.
Match each helper to what it returns.
pairs: a predicate that gives the opposite answer
a function that runs `f` at most one time

steps.prompt: Which of these is **not** a higher-order function?
steps.explain: A higher-order function takes or returns a function. `map` and `setTimeout` take callbacks; the last one does both. Plain addition does neither.

steps.title: Tap and count
prompt: Write `withCount(fn)` that wraps any one-argument function. The wrapper behaves exactly like `fn`, and also has a `calls()` way to find out how many times it ran. Return an object `{ run, calls }`.
template: Dojo.eq("a new wrapper starts at 0", 0, withCount((n: number) => n).calls());

steps.title: Compose a validator
prompt: A rule is `(value: string) => string | null`: it returns an error message, or `null` when the value is fine.
Write `combine(...rules)` that returns one rule which runs every rule and returns the **first** error, or `null` if all pass. Then the tests use it with these rules (already written in the starter):
const maxLen = (n: number) => (v: string) => (v.length <= n ? null : `max ${n} characters`);
starter: const maxLen = (n: number): Rule => v => (v.length <= n ? null : `max ${n} characters`);
solution: const maxLen = (n: number): Rule => v => (v.length <= n ? null : `max ${n} characters`);
template: Dojo.eq("no rules always passes", null, combine()("anything"));
hints: Return a function that loops over `rules`.
Return the first non-null result; after the loop return `null`.
